title: Check yourself: thread lifecycle and states

questions.stem: A reporting service's admin page shows 64 of its 70 threads as RUNNABLE. In a thread dump, most of those 64 have `sun.nio.ch.SocketDispatcher.read0` as their top frame, called from the JDBC driver. What are they doing?

options.text: Queued for a core, since a thread is reported as RUNNABLE while it waits for a processor to run the driver
options.says: RUNNABLE covers ready threads too, but read0 at the top of the stack means the thread waits for the network, not for a core

options.text: Parsing rows, since a thread is reported as RUNNABLE while the driver decodes rows inside read0
options.says: read0 is the native socket read; a thread there waits for bytes from the database (price-call shows 0 ms of CPU in the same call)

options.text: Waiting for the reply, since a thread is reported as RUNNABLE while it is blocked in the driver's read0
options.says: the JVM doesn't see inside a system call, so a platform thread waiting in a socket read is reported RUNNABLE

options.text: Spinning, since a thread is reported as RUNNABLE while the driver repeats read0 in a loop
options.says: read0 is a native socket method, and a thread in it waits for the network rather than repeating a call

origin.section: RUNNABLE Means the JVM Isn't Holding the Thread Back, Not That It Is Using a CPU

questions.stem: During the month-end run, an invoicing service's admin page reads ThreadMXBean: all 120 pool threads are WAITING, none is BLOCKED, and the lock each one waits for is the same `ReentrantLock$FairSync`. What does that say about the pool?

options.text: Idle between invoices, since a pool's queue keeps its idle workers WAITING on a ReentrantLock$FairSync
options.says: an idle worker waits on its queue's ConditionObject; threads whose lock is a ReentrantLock$FairSync wait for whoever holds that lock

options.text: Stuck behind that lock's holder, since a thread waiting for a held ReentrantLock$FairSync is parked as WAITING
options.says: a ReentrantLock parks its waiters, so they are WAITING rather than BLOCKED, and all of them wait for its holder

options.text: Waiting for that lock's timeout, since a FairSync parks each thread as WAITING until its time limit runs out
options.says: a wait with a time limit shows TIMED_WAITING; WAITING means no timeout, and these threads wait for the lock's holder to unlock

options.text: Waiting for that lock's notifyAll(), since a thread WAITING on a ReentrantLock$FairSync is inside Object.wait()
options.says: a ReentrantLock parks its waiters; they go on when the holder unlocks, not on notifyAll()

origin.section: BLOCKED Means Waiting for a synchronized Monitor; a Thread Waiting for a ReentrantLock Is WAITING

questions.stem: To go easy on the database, an audit job calls `Thread.sleep(30_000)` between two batches, inside `synchronized (accounts)`. Transfer threads call methods that are also `synchronized (accounts)`. What does a thread dump taken during the 30 seconds show for the transfers?

options.text: TIMED_WAITING like the audit job, since threads that share a monitor share its waiting state
options.says: each thread has its own state; threads that can't enter a monitor someone holds are BLOCKED

options.text: RUNNABLE and working, since sleep() releases the monitor until the audit job wakes up again
options.says: only Object.wait() releases the monitor while waiting; sleep keeps it

options.text: WAITING for the audit job, since a thread held up by a sleeping thread is parked until it wakes
options.says: threads waiting to enter a synchronized block are BLOCKED, not parked

options.text: BLOCKED behind the audit job, since a sleeping thread keeps the monitors that it holds
options.says: sleep gives up the processor, not the monitor, so the transfers wait to enter for the whole 30 seconds

origin.section: Spot the Problem: a Back-Off That Holds the Cache

questions.stem: Five driver threads are in `board.wait()`. A dispatcher enters `synchronized (board)`, posts a job, calls `board.notifyAll()`, and then spends two seconds writing an audit record before it leaves the block. During those two seconds, what state do the drivers show?

options.text: BLOCKED, since each driver must own the board's monitor again before its wait() can return
options.says: a notified thread goes from WAITING to BLOCKED until it gets the monitor back, and the dispatcher still holds it

options.text: WAITING, since the drivers stay inside wait() until the dispatcher leaves its synchronized block
options.says: notifyAll() takes them out of WAITING at once; while the dispatcher holds the monitor they are BLOCKED

options.text: RUNNABLE, since notifyAll() lets each driver's wait() return while the dispatcher still holds the board
options.says: wait() returns only once the thread owns the monitor again; while the dispatcher holds it, the drivers are BLOCKED

options.text: TIMED_WAITING, since a notified driver's wait() turns into a timed wait until the dispatcher leaves
options.says: the drivers called wait() with no timeout, and once notified they are BLOCKED on the monitor, not in a timed wait

origin.section: A Notified Thread Is BLOCKED Until It Gets the Monitor Back
